title: How Chef Harpal Singh Sokhi Built Karigari Into a Culinary Movement
excerpt: The celebrity chef behind 'Namak Shamak' has expanded his restaurant Karigari to 11 outlets across India, blending regional traditions with modern dining.
body:
• Chef Harpal Singh Sokhi's restaurant Karigari has grown from a single Noida outlet in 2022 to 11 locations across Delhi, Gurugram, Faridabad, Dehradun, Bengaluru and Indore, with plans to reach 50.
  • The menu draws from pre-Partition Punjab, Hyderabadi cuisine and regional traditions, with dishes like Lemongrass Butter Chicken and Jalebi Waffles bridging tradition and innovation.
  • Every detail at Karigari tells a story — plates trace the chef's mother's journey from Rawalpindi to Bengal, and tables feature platters shaped like the map of Punjab.

Chef Harpal Singh Sokhi — the turbaned television personality whose "Namak Shamak" catchphrase has become synonymous with Indian cooking — has quietly built something more lasting than a viral moment. His restaurant chain Karigari, launched in Noida's Sector 51 in 2022, has expanded to 11 outlets across six Indian cities and plans to reach 50 within three years, according to Slurrp.

From Fighter Pilot Dreams to the Kitchen

Sokhi's path to the kitchen was anything but planned. In an interview with Curly Tales, he recalled dreaming of becoming a fighter pilot, inspired by a defence airbase near his childhood home. When the age limit for the Air Force passed, his elder brother suggested a hotel management course. "Within the first three months, I felt a divine connection to this world," Sokhi told Curly Tales. "I decided I would become a chef."

Decades of hotel experience, bestselling cookbooks and hit television shows — from Turban Tadka to Laughter Chefs — followed before Sokhi channelled everything into Karigari, which he co-founded with partners Yogesh and Manish Sharma.

A Menu That Tells Stories

Karigari's menu reads less like a conventional restaurant offering and more like a travelogue. The chef refers to his kitchen team as "Karigars" — artisans — and every section carries his signature irreverence. Starters fall under "Chota Moo Badi Baat," featuring everything from Mumbai's Ragda Patties to Banaras' Tamatar Ki Chaat and Lahori Tawa Taka Tak. The soups section is labelled "Sudkiyaan Maar Ke Piyo Ji," inviting diners to slurp without pretence, according to Slurrp.

"The vision behind Karigari was to blend traditional Indian flavours with modern culinary techniques, creating an innovative dining experience. We aim to honour the craftsmanship in cooking."

— Chef Harpal Singh Sokhi, speaking to Slurrp

The menu draws from Sokhi's training under descendants of Hyderabad's Nizam family, yielding dishes like Pakki Hyderabad Gosht Biryani alongside innovations such as Lemongrass Butter Chicken and Jalebi Waffles topped with rabdi.

Storytelling Beyond the Plate

The attention to narrative extends to every physical detail. According to Curly Tales, plates at Karigari trace Sokhi's mother's journey from Rawalpindi to Bengal, while every table holds a platter shaped like the map of Punjab containing a special spice mix once prepared in Punjabi households. Menu items include his wife's recipe for Suhaagraat Wali Kheer and his mother's Masoor Dal di Roti.

"Karigari is not just my restaurant," Sokhi told Curly Tales. "It belongs to my mother, my wife, my father, and all the mothers in the country."

An Ambitious Expansion

Yogesh Sharma, CEO and co-founder, told Slurrp the chain plans to expand to 50 locations within three years, targeting tier-1 and tier-2 cities. "We're not just opening restaurants — we're creating a movement," Sharma said. Sokhi himself spends 10 to 15 days a month in Delhi, training staff and listening to customer feedback despite living in Mumbai.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad, Karigari represents a growing trend of chef-driven restaurants that treat Indian cuisine as a serious culinary tradition rather than a commodity. Sokhi's approach — rooted in regional authenticity but unafraid of innovation — mirrors the dining expectations of a diaspora that increasingly seeks refined Indian food beyond the standard curry-house formula.
